study_options.description: Research doctorate accepts applicants with a bachelor’s degree; no prior MS required. Students entering without a related MS must complete AA MS requirements internally by the beginning of year three.

study_options.title: Aeronautics and Astronautics

study_options.description: Coursework MS; no thesis requirement stated in Bulletin.

study_options.description: Application is open only to active Chemical Engineering MS or PhD candidates.

study_options.description: Research doctorate; some students complete CEE MS requirements during PhD, which is not a separate external application target.

study_options.description: Research degree typically taking 5–6 years; applicants choose the PhD application instead of CS MS in that admissions cycle.

application_procedures.destination: current Stanford student regular external-style degree application

Coterm and internal intermediate petitions remain excluded.

facts.value: AA pages state MS TOEFL 90 / IELTS 7 and PhD TOEFL 100 / IELTS 7. Those TOEFL cutoffs use the prior scale while Stanford has introduced a new TOEFL score scale for tests from Jan 21, 2026. The department page also lists exemptions for US citizen/permanent resident, English first language, English-taught postsecondary degree, or two consecutive years of English-medium experience in the last 10 years.
conditions: Ask the department to confirm 2027 TOEFL thresholds on the new scale before assessment.

facts.value: Full-time Aero/Astro MS has one Autumn 2027-28 cycle with a final December 1, 2026 deadline. A bachelor’s degree and strong technical preparation in engineering, physics, or comparable science are expected; the specific major is not fixed. Submit the online application, USD 125 fee, two-page single-spaced purpose statement, three recommendations (one academic required; two preferred), scanned transcripts, and English score if applicable. No late applications.
conditions: Applications are reviewed holistically; monitor the application checklist.
exceptions: Previously earned AA or closely related MS holders are not eligible for this external MS.

facts.value: GRE is not required and not considered. The department says MS students are typically self-funded; assistantships may be possible and outside fellowships/loans are potential options. Federal student loans require U.S. citizenship or permanent residence. The AA part-time working-professional MS cannot be completed entirely online; some campus coursework is required and the route best suits locally employed students.
conditions: Funding options are not an award guarantee.

facts.value: Aero/Astro PhD has one final Autumn 2027-28 deadline: December 1, 2026. Applicants may apply with a bachelor’s degree; a prior MS is not required. Current Stanford AA MS students who want to add a PhD must finish department paperwork before conferring the MS. PhD entrants without a related MS must add the AA MS internally by petition and approved program proposal at/before beginning year three.
conditions: The internal MS is a PhD progress requirement, not an external admission target.
exceptions: Current AA MS to PhD requires paperwork before MS conferral.

facts.value: PhD application requires online form, USD 125 fee, two-page single-spaced research purpose statement, three references (one academic required, two preferred), transcripts, and English test if applicable. Students in good standing receive support through thesis submission, at least equivalent to a 20-hour RA salary plus tuition for required enrollment; support sources include fellowship, RA, training grants or TA, with Cardinal Care insurance described by the department.
conditions: Summer enrollment requirements vary by department.
exceptions: Department TOEFL cutoff requires confirmation on revised scale.

facts.value: The nonrefundable non-professional graduate application fee is USD 125, due at submission. Eligible applicants may request GRE fee-reduction, program-participation, or school-based waivers before applying; submit at least 10 business days before the program deadline for timely review.
conditions: After payment and submission, the fee is not refundable, including after withdrawal.
exceptions: Waiver eligibility and any limited school-based allotment depend on program/school; late requests are not guaranteed reviewed by the deadline.

facts.value: Standard application requires three academic or professional references, a statement of purpose, experience information and program-tailored supplemental responses. CV/resume, writing samples and other materials vary by program.
conditions: Program-specific page and current directory control each option's supplemental requirements.

facts.value: CEE maintains merit-based financial aid through teaching assistantships, research assistantships, and/or fellowships. Applicants interested in merit-based aid are asked to indicate that interest in the graduate application.
conditions: This describes an application interest signal and possible aid types, not a guaranteed award. Amounts, eligibility and deadlines remain program-specific.

facts.value: Chemical Engineering does not require GRE scores and will not accept them; it publishes no minimum GPA and no required prior field of study or other graduate degree. The department does not accept recommendation letters through Interfolio.
conditions: The 2027-28 external directory lists GRE as not considered for both degrees; applicants still need to meet university English policy and submit department-required materials.

facts.value: Engineering coterm applicants must be current Stanford undergraduates with a declared major,120 units toward graduation (including applicable AP/transfer units), and six non-summer Stanford quarters by intended entry; undergraduate transfer entrants need only two non-summer Stanford quarters. At least one quarter must overlap active undergraduate and graduate careers. Admission/acceptance must precede bachelor conferral. Department deadlines and criteria vary.
conditions: Engineering standard coterm application requires a statement of purpose, a preliminary program proposal, and Stanford-professor recommendations; some departments require GRE or other material.
exceptions: These Engineering eligibility details do not establish eligibility or terms for Doerr coterm options.

facts.value: CS coterm is only for current, registered Stanford undergraduates and requires at least 120 units toward graduation; students on leave are ineligible. Apply no later than the quarter before expected BS completion. Submit Registrar forms, statement of purpose, resume, unofficial transcripts and three recommendation letters; at least two academic and one CS-faculty recommender are recommended. There is no minimum GPA; 3.5 is recommended for non-CS majors, who are also advised to complete four CS core courses or a mix of core/graduate courses. CS limits applicants to three coterm attempts. The 2026-27/2027-28 deadlines are Winter Oct 6 2026, Spring Jan 8 2027, Autumn Apr 30 2027. A USD 125 fee is assessed only if admitted and accepting. No deferral is allowed; late letters can miss committee review and submitted applications cannot be edited.
conditions: Recommended preparation and GPA are recommendations rather than minimums. Coterm funding is limited; course assistantship may be available after graduate-tuition status.
exceptions: Coterm fee is charged only after acceptance of admission offer; this is different from the nonrefundable external graduate application fee.

facts.value: CS MS applicants need a qualifying bachelor’s degree but need not major in CS; the department recommends strong quantitative/analytical preparation and directs applicants to review its CS Foundation requirements. The MS can be coursework-only or include research. HCP is a part-time MS route for full-time employed people; HCP applicants must reside in the U.S., and international HCP applicants must be employed and located in the U.S. A CS MS is not a guaranteed path to the CS PhD.
conditions: Specific undergraduate coursework is recommended, not a mandatory admission prerequisite in the cited department page. HCP and full-time external routes remain distinct.
exceptions: HCP location/employment restriction applies to HCP route, not full-time MS applicants.

facts.value: CS says GRE is not required and is not considered for MS applicants. Its FAQ says TOEFL is required for applicants whose first language is not English regardless of citizenship, with stated exceptions for U.S. citizens/permanent residents, English first language, or an English-instruction degree. The central Graduate Admissions page also recognizes two years of consecutive full-time English-medium professional/educational experience as an exemption; CS MS FAQ does not mention that exemption.
conditions: Do not silently replace either source rule; ask CS admissions whether the central experience exemption applies to CS MS applicants.
exceptions: GRE is not considered.

facts.value: Applicants need a qualifying bachelor’s degree; a CS major is not required, but strong quantitative and analytical skills are important. The PhD is research-oriented, with few course requirements and typical completion in 5–6 years. CS does not require or consider GRE scores. The SOP limit is 8,000 characters including spaces; three references and application checklist items are required. Applicants must choose CS MS or PhD and cannot apply to both in the same admissions cycle.
conditions: Current Stanford graduate and undergraduate applicants use the online graduate application for PhD admission; this is not the coterm route.
exceptions: No CS undergraduate major prerequisite is stated.

facts.value: CS states all PhD students are guaranteed funding while they make satisfactory academic progress. External support must be disclosed and may adjust Stanford’s award. A 50% research assistantship covers 8–10 units of tuition and pays salary; lower 10–40% appointments or other funding combinations provide less tuition allowance/salary. RA availability depends on a faculty member, and students must be registered, in good standing, and satisfy payroll requirements.
conditions: The guarantee is conditioned on satisfactory academic progress; exact stipend and tuition arrangement depends on appointment/fellowship and funding source.
exceptions: External awards can change the Stanford funding package; conflicting funding restrictions can limit stacking.

facts.value: Doerr states full financial support for PhD candidates through fellowships, teaching assistantships and research assistantships. Master's students may be eligible for teaching or research assistantships. This is general school guidance, not an individual award or guaranteed package.
conditions: Specific coverage, duration, amount, summer support, continuation rules, and exceptions must be checked by program.
exceptions: Environmental Social Sciences Bulletin specifies five academic years for students in good standing; support after year five is not guaranteed.

facts.value: EE coterm application periods: Winter 2026-27 Sep 15–Oct 26 2026; Spring 2026-27 Dec 3 2026–Jan 13 2027; Autumn 2027-28 Feb 3–Mar 31 2027. Review follows each deadline; decisions may take up to four weeks. Applicants may apply after 120 units, no later than the quarter before expected undergraduate completion, and need at least one quarter of overlap. GRE is not required.
conditions: Coterm course transfer/eligibility rules are department and Registrar scoped.

facts.value: EE MS is a terminal coursework-based program with 45 units, no thesis, and a typical full-time completion time of 1.5–2 years. It has autumn entry only; deadline for Autumn 2027-28 is Dec 1, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Pacific and offer response is due Apr 15, 2027. Later PhD study requires applying through the separate PhD process.
conditions: The full-time MS route is separate from coterm and current doctoral-student added-MS options.

facts.value: EE PhD has autumn-only admission; Autumn 2027-28 deadline is Dec 1, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Pacific, with decisions in late February and offer response due Apr 15, 2027. An MS is not required; typical completion is 5–7 years. Students in good standing receive full support for the PhD duration: year-one fellowship, usually advisor RA thereafter, full-time tuition, living stipend/salary and 50% Cardinal Care premium subsidy. Conditions include advisor/funding arrangement, 8–10 units during academic quarters, GPA at least 3.0 and timely progress. External tuition-plus-stipend awards typically replace the first fellowship.
conditions: Later assistantship continuation depends on satisfactory progress and faculty funding.
exceptions: External funding can replace or adjust Stanford support.

facts.value: EE does not require GRE. The department requests unofficial transcripts from every attended college, a purpose statement up to two single-spaced pages, three recommendations, and a USD 125 application fee. TOEFL/IELTS is required unless a central Graduate Admissions waiver applies; EE gives TOEFL 90 / IELTS 7 for admission consideration and TOEFL 109 / IELTS 8 to avoid the placement test. Applicants may request both the SoE and department application fee waivers, but only one is granted; EE preference is low-income or first-generation U.S. citizens/permanent residents.
conditions: EE states central office decides all English waivers; confirm TOEFL score scale for 2027 applicants.
exceptions: Late official transcripts/test scores may be processed if unofficial copies were on time; late recommendation letters may miss committee review.

facts.value: School of Engineering departments award graduate fellowships, research assistantships, and teaching assistantships. The Bulletin does not establish a schoolwide funding amount, guarantee, eligibility, or deadline.
conditions: Specific award access, amount, coverage, duration, renewal, and cycle deadline must be checked for the selected program.

facts.value: For 2027-28 entry, if no exemption applies, official TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic is required. Minimum consideration scores: TOEFL 90 before Jan 21 2026 or 4.5 on/after that date; IELTS Academic 7. Score validity is two years. Individual programs may require higher scores.
conditions: University exemption applies if applicant is a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, first-language English speaker, has a qualifying English-instruction postsecondary degree, or has at least two consecutive years of full-time English-medium professional/educational experience in the past 10 years.
exceptions: Scores below the higher placement-exemption threshold require the English Placement Test before enrollment; no exception is stated.

facts.value: Environmental Social Sciences PhD admits for fall only. For the 2027-28 cycle, the application deadline is November 17, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Pacific; applicants must choose the Environmental Behavioral Sciences (EBS) or Global Environmental Policy (GEP) subplan, and late applications are not accepted.
conditions: The Knight-Hennessy application is separate and has its own October 6, 2026 deadline.

facts.value: Geophysics admits to the department rather than an individual advisor or research group. The committee weighs academic achievement, recommendations, statement of purpose, research fit and potential, and work/life experience holistically; it states no minimum GPA. Applicants are encouraged to contact faculty about research fit and upcoming advising capacity. Applicants pursuing the Geophysics MS as a first step toward a PhD are asked to contact potential faculty advisors; applicants with a BS or MS may apply to the PhD.
conditions: The page displayed a 2025-26 date; that date is not used as a 2027-28 deadline. Current 2027-28 deadline and GRE remain sourced from the live directory.

facts.value: Applicants may apply to one Stanford graduate degree program per academic year; the sole stated exception is applying to two Biosciences PhD programs in one application.
conditions: Do not apply this portal rule to coterm, professional-school, or internal add-degree processes without route-specific support.
exceptions: Biosciences PhD programs only.

facts.value: For non-professional graduate admission, applicants must hold or expect before enrollment a U.S. bachelor's degree or recognized international equivalent. Citizens and residents of all countries are eligible; a department may impose additional preparation and selection rules.
conditions: Applicants with non-U.S. credentials may be required to submit a WES evaluation after accepting an offer; it is not required at application.

facts.value: GRE General and Subject test requirements are set program by program as required, optional, or not considered. For 2027-28, the university's earliest valid test date is Sept 1 2021; a program may use a stricter period.
conditions: A program that does not consider GRE will not show GRE scores to its admissions committee.

facts.value: Materials Science and Engineering lists fellowships, assistantships, and loans as graduate funding options. This does not specify a particular award, amount, coverage, eligibility, duration, renewal rule, or deadline.
conditions: Review specific MSE funding pages and individual award rules before stating eligibility or coverage.
Dates are exact entry-term deadlines; HCP dates are separate from full-time. Full-time rows absent here are not assigned a value.
exceptions: BIOE and CEE entries were not present in the captured current directory even though Bulletin inventory metadata says externally admissible; confirm through current department pages.

facts.value: CEE accepts fall graduate applications once annually through Stanford Graduate Admissions. Required materials are uploaded academic records from every college/university attended for at least a year or current degree enrollment, statement of purpose (maximum three single-spaced pages, two recommended), three recommendations, resume/CV, and TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic if no exemption applies. Official transcripts are requested only after an admitted applicant accepts. GRE is not considered; Interfolio recommendations and emailed materials are not accepted. Applicants with related non-CEE backgrounds may apply but may need extra preparatory study after admission.
conditions: PhD purpose statement should address research area and potentially relevant faculty.
English exemptions use the central Graduate Admissions policy.
exceptions: A traditional civil engineering undergraduate major is not mandatory.
Applications cannot be changed after submission.

facts.value: For Autumn 2027 entry, CEE MS, Engineer and PhD applications and supporting materials are due December 1, 2026 at 11:59 pm Pacific Standard Time; the same date applies to coterm MS. Fee waiver requests should be made by November 17, 2026, ten business days before the deadline. Decisions are released February-April 2027; admitted applicants must reply by April 15, 2027. Admitted MS students can request a one-time deferral to the next autumn by June 30, 2027; PhD and Engineer admits cannot use this deferral.
conditions: Late applications are not accepted.
Department page labels the 2027 deadline PST; preserve its published timezone.

facts.value: CEE FAQ still states old-scale TOEFL 90 for School of Engineering MS applicants, while central Graduate Admissions publishes the revised TOEFL scale for tests on/after January 21, 2026. The current application page defers to central TOEFL iBT/IELTS Academic rules and exemptions. Do not apply the FAQ score to a new-scale 2027 applicant without resolution.
conditions: Resolve TOEFL score-scale discrepancy with CEE/Graduate Admissions before automated assessment.

facts.value: CEE MS is a coursework-based degree with core courses, technical electives, seminars and unrestricted electives; thesis and research are not required. It can be finished in three quarters, though most students take four or five. CEE aims to support MS students where possible, usually describing any award in the admission letter. RA positions for MS are rare and usually in the second study year; course assistantships are competitive and generally favor continuing students. Neither is guaranteed.
conditions: Individual MS specializations have separate program plans.
No assistantship or fellowship amount should be inferred.

facts.value: CEE PhD combines coursework and research, requires service as teaching assistant for one course, and averages five to six years. Engineering PhD students in good standing receive support through thesis submission at least equivalent to a 20-hour RA salary plus tuition for required enrollment and Cardinal Care insurance. Support may come from fellowship, RA, training grant or TA; the department/advisor arranges it and cannot require external funding or self-funding as a condition of entry or continuation. Entering PhD applicants are considered for Engineering/Doerr fellowships with the admission application; Stanford Graduate Fellowships are selectively nominated and offer 12 quarters of stipend plus tuition for 8-10 units.
conditions: Funding continuation requires good standing.
Summer enrollment requirements vary by department.

facts.value: CEE Engineer degree is a post-master's professional research route requiring a thesis and approximately one to two further full-time years after the MS. The current external graduate directory explicitly lists CEE Engineer alongside MS/PhD for Autumn 2027 admission, with December 1, 2026 deadline and GRE not considered. CEE says any MS/Engineer support would generally appear in the admission letter; no guaranteed Engineer award or renewal schedule is published on the reviewed funding page.
conditions: A prior master's degree is the normal academic preparation.
Do not present potential support as a guaranteed award.

facts.value: MS&E MS applicants need an engineering or related quantitative degree with multivariable differential calculus and linear algebra. The department expects both this mathematical preparation and general programming before beginning graduate study, while its FAQ specifically requires multivariable calculus before applying and permits general programming after admission or during the MS. Additional statistics, economics and programming are preferred, and work experience is not required. The degree develops quantitative decision, strategy and organizational leadership skills; 45 units can be spread over about three to four quarters.
exceptions: Programming timing differs across department pages; treat it as a preparation/conditional completion issue, not automatic rejection.

facts.value: For Autumn 2027 MS&E MS and PhD, the current directory gives December 1, 2026 deadline and GRE General required with Mathematics Subject optional; the MS page specifies 11:59 pm PST. The department FAQ requires online application, at most two-page single-spaced purpose statement, resume, uploaded unofficial transcripts, recommendation letters and required test scores. New external applicants should include at least one academic recommender. Late applications are refused; MS decisions usually come in mid-March and PhD in mid-February via the application status page. Official scores received after deadline can still be attached if unofficial scores were entered on time, but review after two weeks is not guaranteed.
conditions: GRE requirement is specific to MS&E; no work-experience waiver is offered.
The university English-test exemptions and minimums apply where relevant.

facts.value: MS&E PhD students without external funding are guaranteed course assistantship support while making satisfactory progress; first-year doctoral students typically receive fellowships, and later fellowship/RA possibilities exist. MS funding is not guaranteed: students may apply for quarter-by-quarter course or research assistantships, generally confirmed at quarter start. The department says fewer than 10% of its over-200 MS students receive these appointments, mainly returning students. MS applicants should prepare to self-fund if no appointment is awarded; US federal loans are limited to US citizens/permanent residents.
conditions: PhD support continues only with satisfactory degree progress.
MS appointments are one quarter only and must be sought anew.

facts.value: ICME accepts MS and PhD applications for autumn entry through separate selections in Stanford Graduate Admissions; applicants can choose only one of the two in a given year and an unsuccessful PhD application is not reconsidered for MS. Upload unofficial transcripts for institutions attended for at least a full-time year, CV/resume, three recommendations (at least one academic strongly recommended), statements, and the required program supplement. The supplement asks for advanced course preparation with three mathematics classes required for consideration, professional/research experience and a short lay explanation of goals; PhD applicants identify nonbinding research/faculty interests, MS applicants select a track and explain career goals. GRE scores are not accepted or considered. Official transcripts are required after admission acceptance.
exceptions: An academic reference may be replaced by three professional references when the applicant graduated five or more years ago.
An optional fourth recommender may serve as backup; three submitted letters complete the requirement.

facts.value: The 2027-28 directory lists ICME MS full-time and HCP autumn entry with January 29, 2027 deadline; PhD autumn entry is due December 1, 2026. HCP is only for MS, selected within the application, and is considered in the same pool as full-time MS. Full-time MS is designed for two years and cannot be completed wholly online; MS-to-PhD transition requires a new application. ICME says all PhD students in good standing receive departmental-standard funding through a combination of fellowship, RA and TA; MS funding is not guaranteed.
conditions: The 2027 deadlines come from the live program directory, rather than older FAQ examples.
PhD funding depends on good standing.

facts.value: MS Design requires a science/engineering BS or equivalent and at least one year of professional employment at application submission. A BS-equivalent degree requires a supporting letter from a faculty adviser or department representative of the awarding institution. No specific design employment is required, but applicants must demonstrate a usable skill toolkit and design potential through a required digital portfolio URL. The Autumn 2027 application is due December 1, 2026 at 11:59 pm Pacific Time with a two-page maximum purpose statement, three recommendations, unofficial transcripts, applicable English results and portfolio; GRE is not required/considered. Decisions are sent by end of March 2027.
exceptions: Applicants with under one year of professional employment are not considered.
Portfolio has no fixed project-count or format rule.

facts.value: MS Design is a full-time six-quarter, two-academic-year project-based degree, with core design courses, methods/domain focus, and a year-long capstone. It is not in session during summer. The program uses Stanford Graduate Engineering 8-10 unit tuition rate; this page does not itself publish a 2027-28 amount. MS Design students are offered course assistantships upon acceptance to offset attendance cost, but offer terms vary each year. Knight-Hennessy is a separate application with October 6, 2026 1 pm Pacific deadline for the 2027 cohort.
conditions: Do not infer a fixed assistantship amount, duration or renewal rule.
Knight-Hennessy is separately selected and is not automatic admission funding.

facts.value: Bioengineering MS and PhD accept applicants with an eligible bachelor's degree or equivalent without a department minimum GPA, prescribed undergraduate field or prior graduate degree. GRE is not considered. Applicants submit the online form, uploaded unofficial academic records including transcript legends, a statement of purpose of at most three single-spaced pages (two recommended), three recommendations, resume/CV and applicable English result. Official transcripts are requested only after admission is accepted; late materials may not be reviewed.
exceptions: No specific undergraduate major is required.
Older BioE page still labels Fall 2026; current 2027 deadlines come from live directory.

facts.value: The live Graduate Admissions directory lists both Bioengineering MS and PhD for Autumn 2027-28 with December 1, 2026 deadline and GRE General/Subject not considered. Department review is holistic; virtual interviews are by invitation. BioE timeline says PhD decisions usually arrive by early March, MS decisions by early April, and admitted applicants start in September. Deferral requests are considered individually for no more than one year, generally for military, medical, visa or education reasons; this statement was posted with the older Fall 2026 cycle and must be rechecked for a 2027 offer.
conditions: Apply 2027 directory deadline, not the older 2025 date still shown on department site.

facts.value: The Bioengineering MS combines core quantitative biology/systems courses, technical electives, seminars and unrestricted electives with an individually planned focus and faculty adviser. It is expected to take about one year and has no thesis requirement. Named areas such as biomedical computation and imaging are examples of focus, not separate admission targets.

Bioengineering PhD research and coursework generally take five to six years; first-year students can rotate through three labs before selecting an adviser, and teaching assistant service for two courses is required. Competitive preparation includes strong quantitative mathematics/physical science and biology from coursework or research, but the department states no fixed pre-application course list. Engineering/Medicine fellowships are considered with the PhD application; Stanford Graduate Fellowship requires nomination and can provide a quarterly stipend plus 8-10 unit tuition for 12 quarters. Training-grant availability varies annually and PhD aid notifications are sent in March/April. These are selective opportunities, not guaranteed individual awards.
conditions: Specific fellowship nomination and grant availability govern an individual award.

facts.value: Chemical Engineering MS is offered externally only through the part-time Honors Cooperative Program, not as a full-time MS. HCP accepts spring and autumn entry; current 2027-28 directory and department page list January 8, 2027 for spring and April 2, 2027 for autumn. The HCP application needs an online form, two-page purpose statement, three recommendations, education/test information and uploaded unofficial transcripts; Interfolio is excluded. GRE is not accepted. Related non-ChemE majors may apply but may need extra background study after admission. The department says it cannot offer financial aid to MS students, and Knight-Hennessy does not cover this part-time route. Decisions follow within about a month after the application deadline.
conditions: The page calls submissions rolling but says final decisions follow completion of the deadline pool.
Full-time MS admission is not offered.
exceptions: Non-traditional major is not automatically disqualifying.

facts.value: Chemical Engineering PhD accepts bachelor-level entrants for Autumn 2027; prior MS and fixed undergraduate major are not required. The December 1, 2026 11:59 pm PST deadline applies to all components including three references. Submit the online application, uploaded unofficial transcripts, purpose statement up to two single-spaced pages, one-page research-experience list in the portal Resume/CV field, recommendations and applicable English scores. GRE is neither required nor accepted. Applicants from varied STEM fields are eligible; the committee values quantitative mathematics/physical-science preparation, biology and relevant ChemE concepts. Faculty do not directly admit applicants to their labs; applications cannot be updated after submission and late recommendations are not reviewed. Decisions usually arrive January/February.
exceptions: The portal describes a three-page CV field, but department specifically limits the research-experience list to one page.
No prior MS or exact course checklist is an eligibility prerequisite.

facts.value: Chemical Engineering PhD students in good standing are funded through thesis submission at least to the School of Engineering standard of 20-hour RA salary, tuition for required registration and Cardinal Care health insurance. Support can be fellowship, RA, training grant or TA and is arranged by the department/adviser; the student cannot be required to self-fund or obtain an external fellowship to enter or continue. The exact individual funding mix can vary by quarter.
conditions: Continued funding depends on program good standing.

facts.value: Materials Science and Engineering accepts autumn MS and PhD applications through Stanford Graduate Admissions. For 2027 entry, PhD is due December 1, 2026 and MS January 12, 2027; GRE General/Subject are not accepted. Required materials include online application, unofficial transcripts/record legends, CV, purpose statement of no more than three single-spaced pages (two recommended), three signed institutional-letterhead recommendations with contact details, and applicable English test results. Official transcripts are required after accepted offer. PhD decisions usually arrive by late January, MS by early March; admitted students must reply by April 15, 2027. Deferrals up to one year are case-specific, usually military, medical, visa or education-related.
conditions: Late applications are refused and late supporting materials may not be reviewed.

facts.value: MSE welcomes MS/PhD applicants from engineering, related science and mathematics degrees; a prior materials major is not required. External applicants cannot apply directly to the MSE Engineer degree, which admits internal candidates only. The MS is intended as terminal study; applicants seeking both MS and PhD should apply for PhD, and may request MS consideration in the application if PhD admission is not offered.
exceptions: Internal Engineer is a different selection route from external MS/PhD.
MS reconsideration of a PhD applicant requires the applicant to opt in and remains discretionary.

facts.value: MSE guarantees PhD students in satisfactory degree progress tuition, living stipend/salary and health insurance subsidy for the program duration; external fellowship support is topped up to department standard if insufficient. The department financial-aid page says MS students do not receive fellowships and are rarely RAs, while its FAQ says a limited number of MS fellowships may be awarded after competitive merit review. Treat MS fellowship availability as an official-source conflict, with no guaranteed award; ask MSE admissions which statement governs the 2027 cohort.
conditions: PhD continuation requires satisfactory degree progress.
Resolve the conflicting MS fellowship statements before showing a categorical no-awards rule.

facts.value: Mechanical Engineering MS applicants need a BS in engineering, physics or comparable science; an applicant who has completed or entered a Mechanical Engineering or closely related master's program, or equivalent international degree, is ineligible for the external MSME. The application requires online form, fee, two-page single-spaced purpose statement, MS supplementary responses, CV, three letters (at least one academic, two preferred), unofficial transcripts for institutions attended for at least a year, and applicable English test. GRE is not accepted through January 2027. The Autumn 2027 full-time application is due December 1, 2026; HCP has separate winter/spring windows in the live directory.
exceptions: Already enrolled in a related master's, not only a completed degree, triggers the MS exclusion.
HCP part-time deadlines must not be replaced by the full-time deadline.

facts.value: Mechanical Engineering PhD applicants need a BS in engineering, physics or comparable science and apply via Stanford Graduate Admissions with online form, fee, two-page single-spaced purpose statement, PhD supplement (research/faculty interests and short prompts), CV, three letters (at least one academic), unofficial transcripts and applicable English results. GRE is not accepted through January 2027. Autumn 2027 entry is due December 1, 2026. The department also lists winter 2026-27 and spring 2026-27 deadlines, but applicants must contact mechanical@stanford.edu before starting or submitting those off-cycle applications.
exceptions: Winter/spring PhD start is conditional on prior department contact, not an open general entry route.

facts.value: Mechanical Engineering MS is coursework-based with no thesis required; the department offers research credit by faculty arrangement. The PhD is research-intensive. ME selectively awards entering graduate fellowships, typically to PhD students; School/department awards commonly provide 8-10 units of tuition and a quarterly stipend for three to five quarters. RAs typically cover 8-10 units and salary for 20 weekly research hours, while TAs/CAs are mainly for continuing students and a limited number of entrants. These are potential funding arrangements, not an unconditional MS award or a fixed multi-year offer.
conditions: Actual award and continuation depend on the offer, faculty funds and appointment terms.

facts.value: Aeronautics and Astronautics Engineer degree is an internal continuation/transfer after an MS. Students submit a Graduate Program Authorization Petition, purpose statement describing thesis topic and a faculty letter confirming preparation and willingness to advise, several weeks before the end of their current degree. This is not a 2027 external application target.

value.A3i6E: The Bulletin outlines the university’s basic requirements for the master’s degree. value.A3i6E: The Doctor of Philosophy (AA-PhD) degree is intended primarily for students who desire a career in research, advanced development, or teaching. This ensures that students have access to advisors and mentors, laboratories, and other resources that support timely progress towards completion of degree requirements. Additionally, being on campus ensures that students are part of the academic and campus community, which supports continued professional development.

The curriculum comprises core bioengineering courses, technical electives, core seminars, and unrestricted electives. Core courses focus on quantitative biology and biological systems analysis. There is no thesis requirement for the MS degree. Coterminal Master’s Program in Bioengineering This option is available to Stanford undergraduates who wish to work simultaneously toward a BS one major and an MS in Bioengineering. The degrees may be granted simultaneously or after different quarters, though the bachelor’s degree cannot be awarded after the master’s degree has been granted. The university minimum requirements for the coterminal program are 180 units for the bachelor’s degree plus 45 unduplicated units for the master’s degree. value.A3i6E: Bioengineering is jointly supported by the School of Engineering and the School of Medicine. The facilities and personnel of the Department of Bioengineering are housed in the Shriram Center, James H. Clark Center, the William F. Durand Building for Space Engineering and Science, the William M. Keck Science Building, the Jerry Yang and Akiko Yamazaki Environment and Energy Building, and the Richard M. Lucas Center for Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy and Imaging. The departmental headquarters is in the Shriram Center for Bioengineering and Chemical Engineering. Students are expected to enter with core competencies in mathematics, biology, chemistry, physics, computing, and engineering. Students entering the program are assessed by examining their undergraduate transcripts and research experiences. Specifically, the department requires that students have completed mathematics through multivariable calculus and differential equations, completed a series of undergraduate biology courses, and completed physics, chemistry, and computer sciences courses required of all undergraduate majors in engineering.

This is done through coursework with specialization in an area of the field, including biomedical computation, regenerative medicine and tissue engineering, molecular and cell bioengineering, biomedical imaging, and biomedical devices. The PhD is conferred upon candidates demonstrating substantial scholarship and the ability to conduct independent research. The program prepares students to make original contributions to bioengineering and related fields through coursework and guided research.
value.advisingExpectations: The Department of Bioengineering is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. Graduate Advising provides a statement of university policy on graduate advising. Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. The department’s intranet provides information and suggested timelines for advising meetings in the different stages of the doctoral program. PhD students are initially assigned a program academic advisor based on the interests expressed in their application. This faculty member provides initial guidance in course selection, exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways, and identifying doctoral research opportunities. PhD students are encouraged to take advantage of three research rotations during this first year, before matching with a dissertation advisor. The research advisor assumes primary responsibility for the student’s future direction, taking on the roles previously filled by the program advisor and ultimately directing the student’s dissertation. Most students find an advisor from our department’s primary faculty members. However, the research advisor may be a faculty member from another Stanford department who is a member of the Academic Council, familiar with supervising doctoral students, and able to provide both advising and funding for the duration of the doctoral program. When the research advisor is from outside our department, the student must identify reading committee members from the BioE faculty. Matching with a dissertation advisor is an essential milestone in the PhD program and is required for making satisfactory degree progress and maintaining good standing. Upon matching with an advisor, students transition from department fellowship to advisor-provided funding. Therefore, students must select an advisor who can financially support them. Students are encouraged to complete three rotations and are expected to submit a thesis advisor agreement by the end of the spring quarter. Students may submit a petition for a 4th rotation to be reviewed and approved by the DGS. PhD students who do not match with an advisor by the end of the 4th quarter of study at Stanford are subject to dismissal from the program. MCL faculty may not be the primary advisors of students. Although a co-advisor from the MCL line is permissible in some situations, the primary advisor must provide at least 50% of the mentoring for the student. Evidence that a student is receiving greater than 50% of mentoring from the primary advisor includes full attendance of lab meetings, regular one-on-one meetings, dedicated space in the primary advisor’s lab, funding provided by the primary advisor, and research being performed in an area that is of current relevance to the primary advisor. Advising situations that do not meet these criteria are subject to review by the graduate studies committee. PhD students may need to change advisors after initial alignment due to unexpected circumstances. Since an advisor is necessary for continued funding and good standing, please consult the Director of Student and Academic Services or the Director of Graduate Studies as early as possible to ensure proper coordination and uninterrupted support. Additional guidance is available in this resource . If a student needs to change advisors, the Department requires the student to actively seek and find a new advisor within one quarter to satisfy minimum progress requirements of the Department and the University and continue enrolling. If the student is unable to secure a new advisor by the end of the quarter, the Department will initiate procedures for dismissal per the “ Guidelines for Dismissal of Graduate Students for Academic or Professional Reasons ” in the Stanford Bulletin. Throughout the PhD, each student must complete an annual Individual Developmental Plan (IDP), usually in the Summer. The IDP is then discussed with the research advisor as a way to facilitate: advising the student, both during and beyond the PhD; establishing clear expectations on both sides concerning degree progress and timely graduation; and emphasizing the importance of wellness in graduate school, together with access to university wellness resources. The Faculty Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) is also available during the academic year by email and during office hours. The department’s student services office is also an essential part of the doctoral advising team: they inform students and advisors about university and department requirements, procedures, and opportunities, and they maintain the official records of advising assignments and approvals. Students are encouraged to talk with the DGS and the student services office as they consider advisor selection or for guidance in working with their advisor(s).

value.A3i6E: The Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) at Stanford conducts fundamental and applied research to advance the civil and environmental engineering professions, educate future academic and industry leaders, and prepare students for careers in professional practice. Civil and environmental engineers work to protect and sustain the natural environment while creating and maintaining a resilient and sustainable built environment. Civil and environmental engineers are essential to providing the necessities of human life, including water, air, shelter, infrastructure, and energy, in increasingly more efficient and renewable ways. Combining rigorous coursework with novel research mentored by Stanford faculty, the PhD program enables students to develop as independent intellectual leaders working at the interfaces between engineering and sustainability.

value.advisingExpectations: Faculty advisors serve as intellectual and professional mentors to their graduate students. They are expected to provide knowledgeable support concerning policies for graduate studies, help prepare their students to be competitive for employment, maintain a high level of professionalism, and establish expectations concerning advisor/advisee relationships consistent with university and department standards. General university policies on advising and the conduct of research can be found on VPGE’s Advising Initiative website. It is important to distinguish between master’s and doctoral advising. Master’s students are assigned academic program advisors. Students can request a specific faculty member in the same program to advise them. Doctoral students and their faculty advisors are expected to discuss and agree on a meeting format. The discussion should include meeting frequency and possible deliverables at the meetings. They should agree on how degree progress will be monitored, for example, through an annual review process or regular meetings with advisors and the GQE or dissertation thesis committee. They should also discuss all the requirements of the PhD degree, including expectations for the General Qualifying Examination, how and when to select and convene the dissertation reading or thesis committee, how and when to decide whether a student is ready to graduate, and when to take the University Oral Examination. PhD students are empowered to request an appointment with their advisor at any time to discuss possible problems with their studies or changes in their academic plans. If students have difficulty meeting with their advisor, they are encouraged to ask the student services team or the directors of graduate studies for advice or assistance. See Graduate Advising for a statement of the university policy on graduate advising. Aligning with a Faculty Advisor In most cases, students are admitted to the PhD program with an initial advisor for their first quarter but not a permanent faculty advisor. To help students explore the range of research activities in the department and facilitate their alignment with a permanent faculty advisor, the department allows students without a permanent advisor to conduct research with a different CEE faculty member during subsequent quarters of the first year of the PhD. The advisor must agree before the student can move into their lab group. To remain in good standing, all PhD students must align with a permanent faculty advisor in the CEE department by the end of their fourth quarter in the PhD program (typically the Summer quarter). It is the student’s responsibility to find a permanent advisor. Faculty members are more likely to accept the responsibility of supervising the research of a student with whom they have worked during research rotations and whose abilities, initiative, and originality are fairly well known to them. Agreeing to work together on a dissertation research project is a serious commitment between a student and an advisor. On occasion, some PhD students are admitted with a permanent advisor specified who will support the student’s funding and research upon enrollment and for the duration of the PhD. This arrangement will be noted in the admission letter. The letter will also specify any other explicit deadlines or requirements. The principal or primary doctoral program or doctoral dissertation advisor must be a CEE faculty member or CEE courtesy faculty member who is a member of the Academic Council. Aligning with an advisor is an essential milestone in the PhD program and is required for making satisfactory degree progress and maintaining good standing. value.A3i6E: ICME is a degree-granting (MS/PhD) interdisciplinary institute at the intersection of mathematics, computing, engineering, and applied sciences. ICME was founded in 2004, building upon the Scientific Computing and Computational Mathematics Program (est. 1989). At ICME, we design state-of-the-art mathematical and computational models, methods, and algorithms for engineering and science applications. The program collaborates closely with engineers and scientists in academia and industry to develop improved computational approaches and advance disciplinary fields. In particular, it leverages Stanford’s strength in engineering applications in the physical, biological, mathematical, and information sciences and has established connections with nearly 20 departments across five schools at Stanford. The program identifies research areas that would benefit from a multidisciplinary approach in which computational mathematics is critical. This multidisciplinary intellectual environment is a core strength of ICME, with interaction among students and faculty with diverse backgrounds and expertise. Students and faculty are active in many research areas: aerodynamics and space applications, fluid dynamics, protein folding, data science, including machine learning and recommender systems, ocean dynamics, climate modeling, reservoir engineering, computer graphics, financial mathematics, and many more. The program trains students and scholars from across Stanford in mathematical modeling, scientific computing, and advanced computational algorithms at the undergraduate and graduate levels. Courses typically provide strong theoretical foundations for solving real-world problems and numerical computations to facilitate the application of mathematical techniques and theories. Training offered includes matrix computations, computational probability and combinatorial optimization, optimization, stochastics, numerical solution of partial differential equations, parallel computer algorithms, and new computing paradigms. ICME offers service courses for undergraduates and graduate students to fulfill departmental requirements, core courses for master’s and doctoral students in Computational and Mathematical Engineering, and specialized electives in various application areas. The ICME master’s program offers a general Computational and Mathematical Engineering track as well as three specialized tracks: Data Science, Imaging Science, and Mathematical and Computational Finance. Prerequisites Fundamental courses in mathematics and computing may be needed as prerequisites for other courses in the program. Check the prerequisites of each required course. Recommended preparatory courses include advanced undergraduate-level courses in linear algebra, probability, differential equations, stochastics, and numerical methods and proficiency in programming. Financial Assistance The department awards a limited number of fellowships, course assistantships, and research assistantships to incoming graduate students. Most course and research assistantships are awarded to students in the doctoral program in ICME. If there are insufficient PhD students to staff all course and research assistantships, these positions may be open to master’s students. However, master’s students are not guaranteed financial assistance.

value.A3i6E: Welcome to Design! The DESIGN-MS bulletin outlines 2026-2027 degree requirements for students pursuing the Master of Science degree (MS) from the School of Engineering . The degree is administered by the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford (The Stanford d.school). 100% completion of all degree requirements within this engineering program, along with meeting Graduate Academic Progress , can lead to the conferral of the Master of Science in Design (DESIGN-MS). Master of Science (MS) Design students (nicknamed Loftees) will develop a strong practice in human-centered design abilities, making, creativity, and applied project work in their chosen domain. The first year foregrounds a structured design practice that pushes to stretch intellectually and grow their skills as makers across mediums. Students will advance in focus through choosing one method and identify a domain focus. A Method will allow students to gain a depth of practice in a select set of mediums. The Domain area will allow exploring challenges in different disciplines where designers can have an impact, and where there are increasing academic and professional opportunities. The degree prepares students for further study in design, design careers in public or private sector institutions, entrepreneurial endeavors, and even careers that may not yet exist.

value.ItCSB: The DESIGN-MS program has a foundation of four pillars: Make, Care, Adapt, and Spark [1] MAKE: The knowledge and ability to prototype and make across a wide range of mediums, existing and emerging. Students can contextualize and apply design principles across disciplinary domains. They have broad material literacy and can build and analyze in many mediums, like physical products, code, policy, and emerging technologies. Learning goals: Experiment rapidly at low resolution using a wide range of physical and digital mediums Recognize emerging technologies that may impact design work Build professional fluency in a subset of design methodologies Investigate needs and opportunities in multi-stakeholder systems Apply foundational design abilities and processes to challenges in other disciplines [2] CARE: The care and responsibility to be leading stewards of the planet, all people, and the data we generate. Students know how to work slowly and fast, with appreciation and respect for varying time scales of change. They learn from and with other humans and the environment. They realize the importance of equity, ethics, and implications. They prioritize people and the planet over profit. Learning goals: Scope a design project that meets a societal or planetary need in relation to the context, constraints, time scale, and opportunities of the problem space Use equitable and inclusive research approaches focused on learning from/with others Predict implications, and impact, of work on complete systems and alternative approaches Consider ethical questions and implications to design work on multiple time horizons Integrate historical, environmental, cultural, and contextual awareness into design work [3] ADAPT: The flexibility of adaptive learners. Students can synthesize and integrate ideas and experiences from across the different aspects of their Stanford education and beyond. They can articulate their capacity and needs as learners when tackling open-ended problems. As emerging leaders, they can establish the conditions for others’ creativity to emerge. Learning goals: Navigate ambiguous projects and processes with appropriate methods Develop a reflective practice on past learning and work to consolidate skills and knowledge Integrate learning from a wide range of life experiences to develop habits and mindsets that foster life-long learning and essential preparation for tackling emergent design opportunities Overcome emotional or intellectual disorientation or discomfort in individual and team contexts when faced with the unknown [4] SPARK: The quirky creativity that produces new world ideas. Students see trends, spot new opportunities, and have the courage to try something untested boldly. They relish disciplinary intersections, embrace ambiguity, and can collaborate and communicate with diverse people. They can set visions and paths for them. Learning goals: Synthesize information from disparate sources, quantitative and qualitative Create design experiments that utilize engineering and scientific principles to evaluate the efficacy and impact of new-to-the-world ideas Move fluidly between abstract ideas and concrete details on design projects Collaborate and communicate as a member of a multidisciplinary design team Communicate deliberately with a range of audiences in a variety of storytelling media

Students identify their doctoral research/thesis advisor, pass the qualifying exam, and advance to candidacy before the end of the second year of study. The research supervisor assumes primary responsibility for the student’s future direction, taking on the roles previously filled by the program advisor and ultimately directing the student’s dissertation. Most students find an advisor from among the primary faculty members of the department. The research advisor may alternatively be a faculty member from another Stanford department familiar with supervising doctoral students and can provide both advising and funding for the duration of the doctoral program. When the research advisor is from outside the department, the student still maintains the previous program advisor from the primary faculty to guide departmental requirements and opportunities. The EE Associate Chair of Graduate Education is available during the academic year by email and during office hours. The department’s student services office is also an essential part of the doctoral advising team: they inform students and advisors about university and department requirements, procedures, and opportunities, and they maintain the official records of advising assignments and approvals. Students are encouraged to talk with their doctoral program advisor, the Graduate Student Teaching Advisor, and the Degree Progress Officer from the student services office as they consider advisor selection or for guidance in working with their advisor(s). See the Electrical Engineering Department Graduate Handbook (pdf) for more information. ALIGNING AND CHANGING DISSERTATION ADVISORS Aligning with an advisor is an essential milestone in the PhD program and is required for making satisfactory degree progress and maintaining good standing. Students are able to rotate during autumn, winter, and spring quarters of their first year. Research rotations are meant to allow students to engage in research within labs, explore research areas, and meet other potential advisors. The EE Department manages an optional rotation program in the autumn quarter for incoming EE PhD students. For winter and spring quarters, students must schedule their own rotations. EE PhD students are expected to align with an advisor at the end of their first year. Upon aligning with an advisor, students transition from department fellowship to advisor-provided funding. Therefore, students must select an advisor who can financially support them. PhD students who do not align with an advisor by the spring quarter of their second year of study at Stanford are subject to dismissal from the program. A student who does not align with an advisor by the stated deadline is considered to be “on academic notice” as a warning of unsatisfactory degree progress. The student's progress and efforts will be closely monitored to ensure that they align with an advisor on a reasonable timeline during the quarter of notice. If a student requires an additional quarter, a faculty committee will meet to review the case and decide on possible outcomes. If a student has not aligned with an advisor by the spring quarter of their second year, a possible consequence includes the termination of a student’s study toward a PhD in Electrical Engineering; however, the student may continue to work toward an MS degree. Departmental PhD financial support does not continue. PhD students may need to change advisors after initial alignment due to various circumstances. Since an advisor is necessary for continued funding and good standing, please consult the Electrical Engineering Student Services team as early as possible to ensure proper coordination and uninterrupted support. Additional guidance for students considering an advisor change is available in this resource . If a student needs to change advisors, the Department requires the student to actively seek and find a new advisor within one quarter, to satisfy minimum progress requirements of the Department and the University and to continue enrolling. If the student is unable to secure a new advisor by the end of the quarter, the Department will initiate procedures for dismissal per the “ Guidelines for Dismissal of Graduate Students for Academic or Professional Reasons ” in the Stanford Bulletin.

value.A3i6E: The Department of Materials Science and Engineering is concerned with designing, making, and characterizing new materials that will have societal impact. Materials science and engineering is an interdisciplinary field involving the relationships between structure and properties of materials and how to take advantage of them in applications. Our students and faculty do research down to the infinitesimally small to achieve breakthroughs of global significance, working at the atomic and molecular levels to engineer matter that will enable the materials, devices, and systems essential for cutting-edge solar energy production, energy storage, information technology, medicine, and more. The Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) program is designed to give students a broad and deep understanding of materials science and engineering so that they will have long and fruitful careers as researchers or teachers at the university level. Students who graduate from our program will be among the world’s leading experts in the areas of their dissertation research. They also will have the intellectual tools to move into new research areas as the field grows and develops. The University’s basic requirements for the PhD degree are outlined in the Graduate Degrees section of the Bulletin. Department requirements are stated below. See the Materials Science and Engineering Department website for more information.

value.advisingExpectations: See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising. The Department of Materials Science and Engineering is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee. Students are expected to meet with their PhD dissertation advisor at least once per year. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. They should also be responsive to one another promptly. Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. The MATSCI Graduate Handbook provides information and suggested timelines for advising meetings in the different stages of the doctoral program. This timeline is also reviewed in the MATSCI Orientation held at the start of a student’s doctoral program. The department provides initial advising support through a PhD advising team of 3-4 faculty members and the department chair. Prior to aligning and declaring their dissertation research advisor, incoming PhD students can connect with any member of the PhD advising team These faculty members provide initial guidance in course selection, assist students in exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways, and aid in identifying doctoral research opportunities. MATSCI does not require formal 10-week lab rotations, but students are required to explore research activities with multiple faculty members during the initial phase of their program. Identifying, aligning, and declaring a dissertation research advisor through rotations, shadowing, or other means is an essential marker of degree progress. MATSCI faculty and staff have established a required, one-unit seminar (MATSCI 231) in the autumn quarter of the first year. This course is intended to structure the search, help students identify an advisor, and initiate their new advising/mentoring relationship. PhD students are expected to match with an advisor and submit the Declaration of Advisor Form to the Student Services Office by the end of their second quarter. The research advisor assumes primary responsibility for the student’s future direction, taking on the roles previously filled by the program advisor and ultimately directing the student’s dissertation. Most students find an advisor from the department’s primary faculty members. However, the research advisor may be a faculty member from another Stanford department familiar with supervising doctoral students and can provide research advising and funding for the duration of the doctoral program. When the research advisor is from outside the department, the student must also identify a MATSCI Co-Advisor from the department’s primary faculty to guide departmental requirements, core coursework, and opportunities. The faculty Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) meets with all the doctoral students during the MATSCI Orientation at the start of the first year and is available during the academic year by email and/or appointment. The DGS or research advisor/co-advisor may initiate a meeting at any time with any student they feel could be in academic or research distress. The MATSCI Student Services team plays an essential role in doctoral advising. They inform students and advisors about university and department requirements, procedures, and opportunities, and they maintain the official records of advising assignments and approvals. They oversee the qualifying exam, candidacy, and oral defense exams, academic progress warnings and concerns, degree conferrals, and the final dissertation submission process. Students are encouraged to talk with the DGS and Student Services Director as they consider advisor selection or for guidance in working with their advisor(s). Student Services can discuss how a student can change program/research advisor(s), declare their dissertation reading committee/oral exam committee, and the processes for filing any necessary paperwork. Graduate students are expected to be active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. As such, the department expects students to read the MATSCI Graduate Handbook and other communications that provide deadlines, web links, and other valuable information on graduate degree progress.

PhD and Engineer Degrees The ME Department provides academic advising in support of doctoral student scholarly and professional development. A successful advisor/advisee relationship is significant for students seeking a PhD in the department. The material in this section also applies to students pursuing the Engineer degree. In addition to the goals listed above for all advisor/advisee relationships, the PhD advisor provides advice and guidance on developing research skills, choosing classes that help with the student’s research, identifying and planning research projects, dissemination/publishing the research, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. The PhD advisor serves as the PhD student’s intellectual and professional mentor. Sometimes, a PhD student may be advised by two or more advisors. In these cases, each individual’s roles and goals should be made very clear to all involved. For example, the co-advisors in such arrangements should strive to coordinate and provide non-conflicting advice to the student. The advisee should work to improve and facilitate communication with the two advisors and provide feedback to and from their advisors. In the ME department, PhD students can be admitted to be advised by a specified faculty member or accepted with a fellowship associated with the research rotation program. For the latter, the department initially assigns the student a program advisor. This faculty member provides initial guidance in course selection, exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways, and identifying doctoral research opportunities. Students are required to perform rotations until a PhD research advisor is identified, and they are strongly encouraged to explore research activities with two or three different faculty members during their first academic year. All PhD students seeking a PhD research advisor are encouraged to actively seek out, meet with, and discuss possibilities for PhD advisors. Ideally, these discussions should include possible research projects and the potential for and sources of sustained research funding. PhD students must identify their doctoral research/thesis advisor (and vice versa) before the first year of study ends. Ideally, this should happen within the first nine to ten months. The research supervisor assumes primary responsibility for the student’s future direction, taking on the roles previously filled by the program advisor and the aforementioned research-related advice and ultimately directing the student’s dissertation. Most ME PhD students find an advisor from the department’s primary faculty members. However, the research advisor may be a qualified faculty member from another Stanford department who can provide both advising and funding for the duration of the doctoral program . When the research advisor is from outside the department, the student must also identify a program advisor, called a co-advisor, from the primary ME faculty to guide departmental requirements and opportunities. The co-advisor is also a member of the student’s dissertation reading committee. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.

MS&E master’s students complete breadth as well as depth in MS&E; depth possibilities include: Data, AI, and Decisions: Courses in Data, AI, and Decisions prepare students in the fundamentals of data and decision sciences, machine learning, and artificial intelligence that are transforming operational and strategic decision making in information technology, finance, healthcare, services, manufacturing, and government. The program combines rigorous technical foundations with emerging modern applications. Financial Analytics: Courses in Financial Analytics prepare students for careers requiring analytical rigor and the ability to innovate around market challenges. Example career paths include financial services, risk management, investment management, financial technology and data processing, financial regulation and policy, exchanges and clearing houses, and auditing and compliance. Courses combine the in-depth study of quantitative techniques with practical, hands-on business problem-solving. Students learn to use mathematical models and quantitative tools to solve complex problems in finance practice, exploiting the intellectual ties between finance, operations research, computer science, and engineering. It offers a high level of flexibility and a range of elective courses that allow students to tailor the program to their specific career goals. Required courses immerse students in quantitative methods and deepen their understanding of finance fundamentals. Projects courses feature practical, data-driven team projects and case studies, fostering group learning and peer interaction. Technology and Engineering Management: Courses in Technology and Engineering Management prepare students for careers including product and project management, management consulting, and entrepreneurship. They acquire skills to manage technical organizations, foster innovation, and deal with rapidly evolving technologies and dynamic markets. Specialized coursework is flexible, allowing students to explore and gain depth and understanding of technical organizations to develop a culture of successful innovation and entrepreneurship, along with decision-making methods under uncertainty, financial analysis, and strategic planning. Technology Policy: Courses in Technology Policy focus on the design and analysis of public policies and corporate strategies, especially those with technology-based issues. It features a grounding in microeconomics and modeling approaches. Courses with a policy focus include such topics such as national security, energy and environment, and health care. Students may also self-design a depth area; possibilities for a self-designed depth area include: Computational Social Science: Courses in Computational Social Science teach students how to apply rigorous statistical and computational methods to address problems in economics, sociology, political science, and beyond. Students are prepared for diverse career paths in data science, information technology, and policy analysis. Coursework covers fundamental statistical concepts, large-scale computation, and network analysis. Students can explore topics such as experimental design, algorithmic economics, and machine learning through electives. Decision Analysis and Risk Analysis: Courses in Decision and Risk Analysis prepare students for careers including management consulting, policy analysis, and risk management, applying engineering systems analysis to tackle complex economic and technical management problems in the private and public sectors. They acquire the skills to identify and develop opportunities in uncertain situations while recognizing and hedging the downside risks. Specialized coursework includes the mathematical foundations for modeling in dynamic, uncertain environments to value and manage uncertain opportunities and risks, applications to public policy, and a chance to work on a client project under faculty guidance. Recommended courses include MS&E 250A, 250B, 252, and 355. Energy and Environment: Courses in Energy and Environment are designed for students interested in energy and environmental issues from the perspectives of public policy, non-governmental organizations, or corporations. Recommended courses include MS&E 241, 243, and 394, CEE 207A, 273S, and ENERGY 201A, 201B, 201C, 223, 240, 241, 281 and 291. Health Systems Modeling: Courses in Health Systems Modeling are designed for students interested in health care operations and policy. Courses emphasize applying mathematical and economic analysis to problems in public health policy and the design and operation of health care services. Recommended courses include MS&E 263, 292, and 463, and HRP 263 and 392.
